faq.q: Who can use the Emerging Technology Program?

faq.a: Not as a single rulebook. It has published discussion papers and guidance setting out principles and questions, while existing requirements for validation, data integrity and change control continue to apply.
faq.q: Has the FDA issued binding rules for AI in drug manufacturing?

faq.a: A defined intended use, risk based evidence that the model is fit for it, controls over model changes and training data, designed in human oversight, and records that let an inspector reconstruct decisions.

name: The FDA's View of AI in Drug Manufacturing
blurb: FDA discussion of AI in manufacturing and how sponsors engage.
title: The FDA's View of AI in Drug Manufacturing
answer: The FDA asked industry in 2023 how AI is used in drug manufacturing and what regulatory questions it raises, covering process control, monitoring and quality decisions. Its draft credibility guidance of 2025 then applied to manufacturing uses whenever a model supports a quality decision, and its Emerging Technology Program lets manufacturers discuss novel approaches before filing.

reading.body:
The FDA treats AI in drug manufacturing as a quality question, not a technology question. Its 2025 draft credibility guidance applies whenever a model supports a decision about drug quality, and the Emerging Technology Program exists so manufacturers can raise novel control strategies before they appear in a filing.

The 2023 discussion paper mapped where the agency saw AI entering the plant: process design and scale up, advanced process control, process monitoring and fault detection, and quality control. It also asked about cloud systems, data management, and Internet of Things devices in plants, which are the same questions that decide whether a model's inputs can be trusted at all. Advanced process control, in the agency's own framing, means adjusting process settings automatically to keep a process within its targets.

The practical consequence is procedural. A manufacturing team with a novel AI control strategy should use the Emerging Technology Program before committing that strategy to a filing, because the risk is not that the model is disallowed but that reviewers and inspectors meet it for the first time in an application.

What this does not cover is the outcome. The data records a discussion paper, a draft guidance, and a program for early engagement, and no enforcement action, approval, or rejection that would show how the agency has actually treated a specific manufacturing model. It also gives no numbers on adoption, so it cannot say how many manufacturers use AI in production rather than in pilots.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

The requirement that a person can understand, intervene in, and override AI decisions. Mandated for high-risk uses under the EU AI Act, and only real when the human has the time, information, and authority to actually intervene.

The internal learned variables, weights and biases, that store what a model knows, counted in billions for modern LLMs. Parameter count is the headline size number, and only one of the three scaling inputs.

explainer:
The FDA's 2023 discussion paper asked manufacturers and others how AI is used in drug manufacturing and what the agency should clarify. It covered uses such as process design and scale up, advanced process control, process monitoring and fault detection, and quality control, and raised questions about cloud based systems, data management, the Internet of Things in plants, and how existing regulations apply.

The agency has since folded manufacturing into its broader AI framework: the 2025 draft credibility guidance applies whenever a model supports a decision about drug quality. Its Emerging Technology Program lets companies discuss novel technologies with the agency before including them in applications, reducing the risk that an innovative control strategy surprises reviewers or inspectors.

What the FDA has said

The FDA has set out its thinking on AI in drug manufacturing through discussion papers and guidance that invite industry input and describe the questions it cares about. The consistent themes are that AI should be applied in a risk based way, that the agency expects a defined intended use and evidence proportionate to the model's effect on quality, that models need lifecycle management because they change, and that existing requirements for data integrity, validation and change control still apply. The agency has also described its own interest in advanced manufacturing as a way to strengthen supply.

The questions the agency keeps asking

How will a manufacturer show a model is fit for its use when its behaviour comes from data? How are model changes controlled, and when must the agency be told? How is data used for training governed and kept traceable? How is human oversight designed so that people can intervene? And how will the agency inspect a process in which a model, not a procedure, decided something? The FDA frames these as areas where it wants to hear from industry rather than as settled rules, which is itself a signal about how early this is.

What manufacturers should do with it

Treat the published principles as the inspection checklist of the near future. Write intended use statements, validation plans and change control for AI in the agency's own vocabulary. Engage the agency early for uses that touch product release or critical parameters, through the programmes it offers for emerging technology. And keep the records that answer each of the questions above, because the inspector who asks them will have read the same papers.
